title: Step by step
hookLine: final knowledge is not reached all at once but by gradual training

cards: Nobody reads their first page of music and plays a concerto. Nobody wakes up fluent. It's tempting to hope the inner life works differently: one retreat, one book, one night under the stars, and everything changes.
The seventieth sutta begins with two monks at a place called Kīṭāgiri who refuse the Buddha's advice about meals. It's Bhaddāli's story again, from five days ago, with new names.
But this time the Buddha uses it to say something larger, about how anyone arrives at all.

teach.b: I do not say, the Buddha tells the monks, that final knowledge is reached all at once. It's reached by gradual training, gradual practice, gradual progress. Then he lays out the steps, and they're surprisingly human.
Someone has enough faith to visit a teacher. Having visited, they sit near. Sitting near, they listen and hear the teaching.
Then they remember it, and examine what it means. Examining, they come to accept it, not blindly, but after looking. From acceptance, enthusiasm; from enthusiasm, effort.
With effort, they weigh things up. Weighing, they strive. And striving, they see the truth for themselves.

A dozen steps, and the first is just turning up. The person who went to a meditation group once and sat at the back has already taken the first three. The person who remembered one line from a talk is on step six.
Nobody is asked to leap to the end. Of the two monks who wouldn't listen, the Buddha says only this: how far they have strayed from the teaching. The Dhammapada has a picture for gradual work.
In Max Müller's words: "Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time."
Little by little isn't a lesser path. In this sutta, it's the path itself.

how: Lay Buddhist practice can follow this sutta's order: visiting a temple, teacher or group, listening to talks, keeping simple precepts, and deepening over years.

o: a sudden flash that changes everything
a teacher's secret saved for the very end
gradual, step by step, in due order

games.q: the steps, in the sutta's order: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha says final knowledge comes in a single flash
he says it's reached by gradual training, practice and progress.
the first step in the sutta's list is simply going to a teacher
faith enough to visit, then sitting near, then listening.
the Dhammapada pictures a smith working silver little by little
in Müller's words, 'one by one, little by little, and from time to time.'

games.q: two monks at Kīṭāgiri won't listen to the Buddha's advice. according to the sutta's steps, where are they?
o: far from the goal: they've skipped the early steps
it doesn't matter, as long as they meditate
games.why: listening is one of the first steps, and of these two monks the Buddha says: how far they have strayed.

practice: Ask honestly which step you're on, with any path you're walking: turning up, listening, remembering, testing what you've heard. Don't judge the answer.
Name the very next step, just one, and let the breath come slowly, one after another.

wordCard.voice: Anupubba. Final knowledge isn't reached all at once, the Buddha says, but by gradual training, from simply turning up to seeing for yourself.

orig.note: Pali anupubba: gradual, in due order. the sutta speaks of gradual training, practice and progress.

carryVoice: Your line: just turning up. Nobody is asked to leap to the end. Week sixty-six, done: tendencies, the colt, the quail, four dangers, rebirth, coming back, and step by step.
